name: Mariner 7
payload: Mars flyby spacecraft, two TV cameras and spectrometers (381 kg)
significance: Mariner 7 followed its twin past Mars five days later, reprogrammed in flight to take more pictures of the south polar cap after Mariner 6's intriguing views. It survived a scare days before arrival, when contact was lost and controllers had to switch it to its low-gain antenna. Passing at 3,430 km on 5 August 1969, it returned 93 approach and 33 close-up images. Oddly, the floor of the giant Hellas basin looked smooth and crater-free, and three frames caught the moon Phobos, showing for the first time that it was an irregular lump rather than a sphere.
statusNote: Launched 1969-03-27 22:22:01 UT on an Atlas-Centaur from Cape Kennedy (Siddiqi; NSSDCA). Mid-course correction 1969-04-08; lost high-gain contact on 1969-07-30 and recovered on the low-gain antenna. Closest approach 05:00:49 UT on 1969-08-05 at 3,430 km. It then continued in solar orbit (1.11 x 1.70 AU), returning data until mid-1971; that coast isn't drawn. TRAJECTORY (calculated, drawn dashed): no measured trajectory for this spacecraft is publicly archived (JPL Horizons has no ephemeris for it), so the path is a two-body transfer orbit calculated between Earth at the published launch time and Mars at the published arrival time. For modern direct flights checked against Horizons, arcs calculated this way fall within about 0.002 AU (300,000 km) of the real trajectory, but this one can't be checked against data, so it's drawn dashed.
